newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - U.S. T-bond vols firm, await Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - U.S. T-bond vols firm, await Greenspan.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. Treasury bond options were a touch firmer in late trade as underlying bond prices slipped on news of disappointing two-year Treasury note auction results, dealers said.
Volatilities were also underpinned by caution ahead of Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on Wednesday and some economic data later in the week, they added.
"There might be some selloff on Friday, but the lowest volatility you've probably seen last week," a brokerage trader at the Chicago Board of Trade said.
He noted that volatilities tended to firm up toward the end of a month as the market prepares for the monthly employment report. The February report is due out on March 7.
"We're already in that pre-unemployment pump-up, so they (volatilities) are going to hold," the trader said.
Implied volatilities for CBOT April and June T-bond futures options were slightly above Monday's closing levels at around 9.7 and 9.9 percent.
March T-bond futures slipped into negative territory after results of the Treasury's 17.5 billion two-year note auction came out.
The auction produced a high yield of 5.885 percent, with 94 percent of the bids awarded at the high yield. Bid-to-cover ratio was 2.21 times.
While the selloff in bonds was not so aggressive, growing bearish sentiment raised concerns about Wednesday's five-year note auction and the Greenspan testimony, traders said.
At the shorter end of the yield curve, Eurodollar volatilities were also slightly firmer.
A trader at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange said volatilities started firming in the morning after a big investment bank bought 5,000 lots of September 94.25 puts.
"That started things going a little bit and then the locals started bidding the June," he said.
Implied volatilities for June and September Eurodollar futures options were pegged at around 8.3 and 13.1 percent, up about 0.2 point each.
Traders said apart from Greenspan, auction and economic data, a further slide in the dollar could hurt U.S. asset markets.
"I think that's going to be the preeminent influence in the short term," the CME trader said. "If the dollar gets hit here overnight, we're going to be lower on that."
